title: Reliable nitrogen-fixing microbial partnerships for major cereal crops

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a dependable partnership between major cereal crops and microbes that convert atmospheric nitrogen into nitrogen the plants can use. The goal is to deliver enough nitrogen, at the right stages of crop growth, to supply most crop nitrogen requirements while maintaining commercially competitive yield and quality across varied field conditions. Successful nitrogen fixation inside a microbe is only one part of this capability: the microbes must establish on or within the crop, remain active, and transfer the fixed nitrogen to the plant.

As a conceptual synthesis, this is a microbiological advance whose success also depends on plant physiology, agronomy and fertilizer management. It could involve engineered or selected microbes, changes that support their association with the plant, or delivery systems that improve establishment. Nanocoated bacteria applied to leaves are one reported approach in the supplied research; they do not define the full scope of the innovation.

significance.text: The central conditional benefit is a major new agricultural capability: reliable biological nitrogen delivery to high-yielding cereals. If the partnership supplies most crop nitrogen requirements while preserving performance, it could substantially reduce dependence on manufactured nitrogen fertilizer. The useful measure is nitrogen actually delivered to the crop and fertilizer genuinely displaced over sustained production, rather than microbial activity or improved plant growth alone.

As a downstream synthesis, lower fertilizer requirements could reduce some production costs and environmental burdens associated with fertilizer manufacture and use. Those outcomes would require separate assessment. Inoculant production and application costs, yield, nitrogen losses, other nutrient requirements, adoption and changes in land use would all affect the balance. Biological fixation introduces nitrogen into the agricultural system; it does not by itself guarantee that the nitrogen will be retained, used efficiently or delivered with lower overall environmental impact.

The scale of the proposed change should therefore be understood conditionally. Supplying most crop nitrogen would not mean eliminating all fertilizer or all crop nutrient management, and success in one cereal or environment would not establish reliability across cereal production. A broadly useful partnership would need to sustain its contribution under realistic management and variable field conditions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is the integration of microbial establishment, sustained nitrogen fixation and timely nitrogen transfer into a reliable crop partnership. The supplied proposal identifies fixation's energy demands, oxygen sensitivity and regulation under nitrogen-rich conditions as scientific barriers. These are coherent design concerns, but the retained source contains no inspectable scientific discussion that independently documents them for the reported system.

The engineering challenge extends beyond increasing fixation in an isolated experiment. The partnership must obtain sufficient resources to support fixation without imposing an unacceptable cost on crop performance, provide conditions compatible with fixation, and release or transfer nitrogen in a form and at a time the crop can use. It must also establish reliably and remain productive across soils, climates and fertilizer regimes. These are proposed requirements derived from the concept, rather than demonstrated properties of the cited approach.

A separate measurement challenge is distinguishing newly fixed atmospheric nitrogen from nitrogen already present in the soil or other inputs. Better growth or higher plant nitrogen content alone would not resolve that distinction. The proposed breakthrough therefore requires both a working biological partnership and convincing attribution of its nitrogen contribution, followed by evidence that the contribution permits sustained fertilizer reduction.

current_state.text: The supplied research metadata identifies a report by Yiwen Liao, Li-Mei Zhang and colleagues titled “Stable foliar colonization of nanocoated nitrogen-fixing bacteria enhances crop nitrogen supply,” attributed to Nature Food on 2 January 2026, with DOI 10.1038/s43016-025-01280-2. The research attributes improved foliar colonization and nitrogen supply to this report, including an estimated 27.89% contribution to total plant nitrogen in one experiment and field-trial fertilizer-saving potential. These remain reported findings whose scientific content could not be verified from the retained material.

The supplied review found that the retained copy contains only a cookie-access notice, rather than the article or its abstract. It therefore could not confirm the document's identity from its contents, inspect the experimental scope, or examine the methods and nitrogen accounting behind the 27.89% estimate. This corrects the earlier statement that the numerical result had been checked against the abstract. The source index records a saved, verified artifact, but that does not establish that usable article content was retained. The extraction failure is an access limitation, not evidence that the attributed findings are false.

If verified, a 27.89% contribution to total plant nitrogen would represent partial nitrogen delivery in the reported experiment. It would not, by itself, demonstrate an equivalent percentage reduction in fertilizer requirements, supply of most crop nitrogen, or durable performance across production systems. The supplied material does not resolve the crop, treatment conditions, uncertainty, accounting method or field-trial outcomes needed to interpret that number.

The supplied record does not establish whether broad, durable replacement of most cereal nitrogen fertilizer had been demonstrated by 1 November 2026: its freshness search record is empty. Accordingly, the earlier categorical statement that such replacement remained unproven cannot be retained as a verified assessment of the field at that date. The appropriate conclusion is narrower: the supplied evidence does not demonstrate completion of this innovation, and its overall contemporary status remains unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstrations would include independent, multiyear field trials across major cereals and a deliberately varied set of climates, soils and management systems. The partnership should supply most crop nitrogen requirements while preserving competitive yield and quality with greatly reduced manufactured nitrogen fertilizer. The meaning of “most,” the fertilizer reduction target and acceptable performance margins should be specified before evaluation. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Partnership supplies most cereal nitrogen with competitive multiyear field performance

completion_criteria.text: The proposed evidence package should combine isotope tracing with full nitrogen budgets to distinguish atmospheric fixation from uptake of existing soil nitrogen and other inputs. Suitable comparisons should separate the partnership's contribution from fertilizer effects and background crop performance. Repeated production should also test whether apparent fertilizer savings are sustained rather than achieved by drawing down soil nitrogen reserves. Agreement between nitrogen attribution, crop uptake and maintained performance would make the result more convincing than growth measurements alone.
completion_criteria.label: Nitrogen budgets and isotopes verify sustained atmospheric nitrogen contributions

completion_criteria.text: Reproducibility should include independent teams and deployments, with sufficient reporting of inoculant preparation, application, establishment, nitrogen contribution and variation in outcomes. Practical evaluation should examine delivery reliability, costs, environmental effects and the conditions under which the partnership fails or requires supplemental fertilizer. Finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries; they could not establish literal reliability in every cereal or environment.
completion_criteria.label: Independent deployments reproduce results with costs and practical limits reported

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with MIC-02, “A predictive theory of microbial communities,” and MIC-10, “Programmable microbial consortia for durable ecosystem functions”: both could help explain or design reliable establishment and function in agricultural microbial communities. MIC-04 has the narrower endpoint of nitrogen delivered to cereal crops with useful agronomic performance. It could succeed through a particular partnership without providing a general community theory or a general platform for ecosystem functions.

Conceptual comparison with MIC-06, “A predictive whole-cell model for microbial design,” and MIC-12, “A causal map from microbial metabolites to host phenotypes”: whole-cell prediction could help manage microbial resource allocation and fixation, while causal host–microbe analysis could help connect nitrogen transfer to plant responses. MIC-04 nevertheless requires field-level nitrogen attribution and fertilizer displacement; neither cellular prediction nor an observed host response alone establishes that outcome.

Conceptual comparison with MIC-03, “Routine experimental access to microbial dark matter,” and MIC-01, “An autonomously reproducing cell built from defined components”: access to previously inaccessible microbes could expand the organisms available for crop partnerships, and defined-component cell construction concerns a different level of biological engineering. MIC-04 requires neither routine access to all such microbes nor construction of a cell from defined components, and success in either neighboring concept would not itself establish dependable crop nitrogen delivery.

Conceptual comparison with MIC-07, “Programmable, reversible living therapies in the human microbiome,” and MIC-05, “A general platform for targeted, adaptable phage treatment”: these share questions about delivering biological agents and obtaining reliable function in complex environments. Their therapeutic endpoints and host settings differ from cereal nitrogen nutrition. Reversibility and targeted phage treatment remain distinct capabilities rather than implicit requirements fulfilled by an agricultural inoculant.

Conceptual comparison with MIC-08, “Broadly effective control of bacterial antibiotic persistence,” and MIC-09, “Forecasting horizontal gene transfer and resistance spread in microbial communities”: persistence and genetic change may influence the behavior of deployed microbes, but neither antibiotic persistence control nor resistance forecasting is the defining objective here. Reliable nitrogen delivery would not establish those broader capabilities.

Conceptual comparison with MIC-11, “Quantifying how environmental viruses control biogeochemical fluxes”: both concern microbial influences on nutrient cycling. MIC-11 focuses on explaining viral control of environmental fluxes; MIC-04 focuses on creating a dependable crop-associated nitrogen supply. A successful partnership would not, by itself, quantify viral control of nitrogen cycling or other biogeochemical processes.

brief.title: Grain crops fed by microbes using nitrogen from air
possible: Farmers could grow major grain crops with much less manufactured nitrogen fertilizer while keeping yields and grain quality competitive. Microbes, tiny organisms living on or inside plants, would turn nitrogen from the air into a nutrient crops can use. The partnership would supply most of their nitrogen needs throughout growth.
why: For cereal farmers, this would make biological nitrogen delivery a dependable part of production. It could reduce dependence on manufactured fertilizer and lower some costs and environmental burdens associated with making and using it.

sources.who: Yiwen Liao, Li-Mei Zhang and colleagues
sources.showed: A nanocoating, a very thin protective layer, helped bacteria survive on leaves. The coated bacteria supplied 27.89% of total plant nitrogen in an experiment.
sources.quote: The nanocoating improved bacterial resistance to UV radiation, oxidative stress, aerobic conditions and desiccation, enhancing adhesion and biofilm formation on leaf surfaces.
sources.cited_for: Protecting bacteria can improve their survival on crops and their nitrogen contribution.
sources.not_established: The experiments do not establish reliable delivery of most cereal nitrogen needs across varied field conditions.

sources.who: Allen Van Deynze, Pablo Zamora and colleagues
sources.showed: A traditional maize variety grown in nitrogen-poor fields in Oaxaca obtained up to 82% of its nitrogen from air. Its above-ground roots secreted sugary material that housed bacteria.
sources.quote: High levels of nitrogen fixation are supported, at least in part, by the abundant production of a sugar-rich mucilage associated with aerial roots that provides a home to a complex nitrogen-fixing microbiome.
sources.cited_for: A cereal can obtain most of its nitrogen through a natural partnership with microbes under particular conditions.
sources.not_established: The study does not establish competitive yields with greatly reduced fertilizer across major cereals and varied environments.

sources.who: Rafael E. Venado, Jennifer Wilker and colleagues
sources.showed: Some sorghum varieties obtained about 40% of their nitrogen from air through bacteria on above-ground roots. Bacterial abundance varied with genotype, the plant's genetic makeup, and location.
sources.quote: However, bacterial abundances varied based on the genotype and the location.
sources.cited_for: The root partnership also occurs in sorghum, with outcomes that depend on the plant and its environment.
sources.not_established: The study does not establish reliable replacement of most fertilizer while maintaining commercial crop performance.

sources.who: Layne N. Connolly, Nicola Lorenz and colleagues
sources.showed: Ohio field trials found that maize varieties differed in how much nitrogen they obtained from air. Estimates depended on the comparison plant and fertilizer use.
sources.quote: Up to 36% of plant N was derived from the atmosphere, with values varying by accession, the reference plant used, and the fertilizer level.
sources.cited_for: Nitrogen contributions extend beyond the Oaxaca maize variety, but vary with crop variety, management and measurement.
sources.not_established: The trials do not establish sustained delivery of most crop nitrogen or commercially competitive fertilizer replacement.

shown: Van Deynze and colleagues found that a traditional maize variety could receive most of its nitrogen from air in nitrogen-poor fields in Oaxaca. Work in sorghum and other maize varieties also found contributions. Liao and colleagues improved bacterial survival and nitrogen supply by coating bacteria applied to leaves.
missing: A partnership still needs to supply most crop nitrogen at the right growth stages while preserving competitive yield and quality across varied fields.
Measurements need to show that fertilizer savings persist without drawing down nitrogen already stored in soil.
Independent deployments need to establish practical delivery, costs, environmental effects and conditions where supplemental fertilizer remains necessary.

milestones.label: Most crop nitrogen supplied with competitive field performance
milestones.explanation: Independent field trials over multiple years would have to show that partnerships supply most nitrogen across major cereals with greatly reduced fertilizer and competitive yield and quality. This would establish agricultural usefulness.

milestones.label: Nitrogen tracking confirms a sustained contribution from air
milestones.explanation: Isotopes, distinguishable forms of nitrogen, and accounting of nitrogen inputs and outputs would have to confirm sustained delivery from air. This would distinguish fixation from fertilizer uptake or depletion of soil reserves.

milestones.label: Independent deployments reproduce results and establish practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce results while reporting delivery, costs, environmental effects and failures. This would establish where the partnership works and when extra fertilizer is needed.

uncertain: The thresholds for supplying most nitrogen, competitive crop performance and greatly reduced fertilizer still need to be defined.
The durability of nitrogen delivery across soils, climates and fertilizer regimes remains an open question.
The overall environmental benefit depends on nitrogen losses, production and application costs, and crop performance.

page.title: Nitrogen-fixing microbial partnerships in maize and sorghum
page.definition: Maize and sorghum receive plant-available nitrogen from associated microbes that fix atmospheric N₂, converting the gas into ammonia. The partnerships displace nitrogen fertilizer while maintaining field yield.

goal.need: Wheat, rice and maize together accounted for over 50% of agricultural nitrogen-fertilizer demand in the IEA’s 2014 dataset. Crop-associated nitrogen fixation is being pursued to replace part of the nitrogen supplied as fertilizer.

figures.caption: Global mean nitrogen-fertilizer application in the IEA’s 2014 dataset.
figures.note: These are application rates, not total crop nitrogen requirements.

statements.quote: The project uses traditional breeding to introduce nitrogen fixing aerial root mucilage traits into corn and sorghum cultivars.
statements.context: The statement describes the funded N₂Cereals project.

statements.quote: transfer the nitrogen-fixing ability of legumes into non-legume cereals
statements.context: The stated objective of the global research effort coordinated by Giles Oldroyd, described on 27 April 2022.

completion.title: A cereal partnership cuts fertilizer and N₂O without yield loss over two field seasons.
completion.criterion: In maize or sorghum, a nitrogen-fixing partnership demonstrates all TEOSYNTE targets over two field seasons: nitrogen-fertilizer use falls by >55% in maize or >48% in sorghum; yield remains ≥100% of control yield; and nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions fall by >50% relative to the unmodified control. Field emissions measurements span two full years, including growing and fallow periods.
completion.set_by: ARPA-E, TEOSYNTE funding opportunity DE-FOA-0003405, sections I.D–I.E.
completion.threshold_quote: >48% reduction (sorghum) or >55% reduction (corn) in N fertilizer use;
completion.basis: TEOSYNTE includes microbial nitrogen delivery and designed plant–microbe interactions. Its joint targets provide a published field benchmark for maize and sorghum bioenergy crops. The benchmark measures fertilizer displacement; it leaves the atmospheric fraction of total plant nitrogen unspecified. Grain-quality and environmental-coverage thresholds are also unspecified.

milestones.title: Cereal-associated microbes exhibit nitrogenase activity above negative controls.
milestones.criterion: Cereal-associated microbes reduce acetylene to ethylene above negative controls, demonstrating activity of nitrogenase, the N₂-reducing enzyme. This assay does not quantify crop nitrogen supply. On 12 November 2024, Martinez-Feria et al. reported activity of engineered maize-associated bacteria in culture with 10 mM NH₄Cl (four replicates). On 3 March 2025, Venado et al. reported activity of Klebsiella variicola A3 and Azotobacter vinelandii DJ in sorghum root mucilage (six replicates).
milestones.set_by: Field convention: acetylene-reduction assays, described in ACIAR Monograph 136, chapter 11, and applied in maize and sorghum research.
milestones.threshold_quote: indicating relative rates of nitrogenase activity.

milestones.title: Microbially fixed nitrogen enters cereal chlorophyll above control levels.
milestones.criterion: Nitrogen from supplied ¹⁵N₂ enters cereal chlorophyll significantly above non-fixing-bacterium or unlabelled-gas controls, separating plant assimilation from bacterial attachment. Van Deynze et al., published on 7 August 2018, demonstrated enrichment in maize root chlorophyll extracted as pheophytin (n = 3; p < 0.05). Venado et al., published on 3 March 2025, demonstrated enrichment in sorghum root chlorophyll against a nitrogenase-deficient bacterial control (n = 8; p ≤ 0.001).
milestones.set_by: Field convention: isotope transfer into plant-specific metabolites, applied by Van Deynze et al. in maize and Venado et al. in sorghum.
milestones.threshold_quote: indicating that aerial roots are indeed the sites for transfer of fixed nitrogen to the plants

milestones.title: A cereal obtains a statistically supported contribution of atmospheric nitrogen in field conditions.
milestones.criterion: Cereal tissue shows a statistically supported atmospheric-N contribution by ¹⁵N isotope dilution or natural abundance against non-fixing references, subject to soil-N uptake assumptions. In maize, three Oaxaca fields in 2016–2017 (five blocks) gave estimated atmospheric contributions of 31–55% by isotope enrichment, significant in four of six experiments. In sorghum, 15 genotypes at five Brazilian sites in 2014 (three blocks) gave evidence at two sites, reaching an estimated 78% in shoots. The sorghum estimate used natural abundance.
milestones.set_by: Field convention for isotope attribution, documented in ACIAR Monograph 136, chapter 10, and applied in maize and sorghum field experiments.
milestones.threshold_quote: statistically significant inputs of fixed N

milestones.title: A cereal keeps ≥100% yield over two seasons with >55% less N fertilizer in maize or >48% less in sorghum.
milestones.criterion: For two field seasons, a cereal partnership uses >55% less nitrogen fertilizer in maize or >48% less in sorghum while producing ≥100% of control yield. A Purdue maize experiment in 2021–2022 (eight blocks; six N rates) estimated reductions at maximum yield of 27.4 and 10.5 kg N ha⁻¹ against control optimum rates of 270 and 287 kg N ha⁻¹, respectively. These estimates fall short of the maize target; the 2022 reduction’s 95% confidence interval included zero. The inoculant developer coauthored the study.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-E, TEOSYNTE DE-FOA-0003405, section I.E: fertilizer and yield components of the programme target, published specifically for maize and sorghum.
milestones.threshold_quote: Maintenance of ≥100% yield with N fertilizer reduction;

not_found: No published result satisfying all four TEOSYNTE targets for a nitrogen-fixing maize or sorghum partnership was found.
No cereal-wide completion test combining majority atmospheric-nitrogen supply, yield, grain quality and environmental coverage was found in the ARPA-E, ENSA and UK government material searched.
